extracted.intended_audience: students and readers seeking guidance on clear reasoning, speech, and the foundations of science (philosophy/logic learners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for using speech, names, definitions, and method to reason correctly and to build reliable science; includes causes of error and abuses to avoid. Aimed at improving how one forms, records, and communicates knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty of Invention (seeking causes and effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of regulated Thoughts: (1) seeking the causes or means that produce an imagined effect (common to man and beast), and (2) seeking all possible effects that can be produced by something we imagine (invention), which is peculiar to man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invention (Sagacitas, Solertia) is a 'hunting out' of causes for effects or effects of causes; examples include sweeping a room to find a jewel, a spaniel ranging the field, or running over the alphabet to find a rhyme. This faculty underlies human curiosity and inventive thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remembrance (method of tracing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remembrance consists in running the mind back over places and times where something was last present to find it; a re-conning of former actions (Reminiscentia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When searching for a lost thing, begin at the time and place where it was missed and trace actions and occasions backward to locate when and how it was lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence / Foresight (experience-based prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence (foresight) is forming expectations about future events by recalling similar past actions and their outcomes; more experience yields more reliable expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sequence of past events as 'signes' to predict outcomes, but recognize such conjecture is fallacious if not all circumstances are observed; prudence is presumption, not certain knowledge (prophecy belongs only to God).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs as grounds for inference
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign is an antecedent event of a consequent (or conversely); the more often a precedent has been observed, the less uncertain the sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase confidence in inferences by accumulating repeated observations (experience). The person with the most experience in a business has the most 'signes' for guessing the future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary uses of Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech's general uses: (1) to register the consequences of our thoughts (notes of remembrance), (2) to signify thoughts to others for counsel and teaching, (3) to declare wills and obtain mutual help, and (4) to please and delight by playing with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these four constructive purposes when forming and using language; speech enables memory, communication, cooperation, and ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuses of Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Four corresponding abuses of speech: (1) registering thoughts wrongly by inconstant signification of words, (2) using words metaphorically (out of their ordained sense) to deceive others, (3) declaring as will what is not, and (4) using words to grieve or harm (abusive speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these abuses: be consistent in signification, beware deceptive metaphors in serious reasoning, speak truthfully about will, and do not use speech to injure except to correct when obligated to govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of Names: proper vs universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Names proper (singular) refer to one thing; common/universal names refer to many things unified by similarity. Universals allow generalization from particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use universal names to record general consequences discovered in particulars (e.g., 'Every triangle hath its three angles equal to two right angles') and be aware that universals are names imposed for convenience and reckoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as right ordering of names
rubrics_metrics.description: True and False are attributes of Speech, not of things; truth consists in the right ordering of names in our affirmations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To seek precise truth, remember what each name stands for and place names accordingly; settle significations (definitions) before reasoning to avoid entanglement in words and consequent error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: In geometry (and in solid reasoning generally) begin by settling the significations of words (Definitions). Wrong or neglected definitions multiply errors as reasoning proceeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine and correct definitions of former authors or make your own; flawed definitions lead to absurdities that propagate through subsequent reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-to-names classification (what can be accounted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything that can be entered into an account (added or subtracted) is 'subject to names'. Considerations reduce to four heads: matter/body, accidents/qualities (abstract names), fancies/conceptions (perceptions), and names of names/speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning, be explicit about which consideration (matter, accident, fancy, or speech) you name to avoid category confusion in assertions and arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative names and their use
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative names (e.g., Nothing, No Man, Infinite) are not names of things but useful notes to indicate that a word is not the name of the thing in question; they help correct reckoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use negative names to exclude inappropriate admissions and to remind of past cogitations; they serve corrective functions in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words insignificant (meaningless coinages or contradictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insignificant words are (1) new words without explained meaning (often coined by schoolmen) and (2) composite names whose constituent significations are contradictory (e.g., 'incorporeal body', 'round quadrangle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid or challenge coinages without definitions and reject expressions that combine incompatible significations; such words signify nothing and lead to nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding requires speech-caused conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding is conception caused by speech: when hearing speech produces the thoughts the words were ordained to signify, one understands; without meaningful speech there is no understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure words used actually cause the intended conceptions in listeners; repeating meaningless phrases does not equal understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconstant names (names affected by passions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names for things that affect us (virtues, vices, values) are of inconstant signification because people's affections and prejudices vary: one man's 'wisdom' may be another's 'fear'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using such names as premises in reasoning; they cannot reliably ground ratiocination. Metaphors and tropes are less dangerous because they signal inconstancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason defined as adding and subtracting consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason is nothing but reckoning (adding and subtracting) the consequences of general names; it operates wherever addition/subtraction of parts and wholes is possible (numbers, measures, syllogisms, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply reasoning where parts and wholes can be summed or partitioned; treat reasoning as systematic accounting of names and their consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of Reason (begin at definitions and ensure premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: The use and end of Reason is to begin at definitions (the elements) and proceed methodically to assertions and syllogisms; certainty of conclusions depends on certainty of all antecedent affirmations and negations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept conclusions on trust of authors; fetch them from first items (clear definitions) and check each premise. Example: a master who sums bills without verifying each bill's correctness gains no real knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Error and Absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Error: a deception in presuming something past or future that may simply be false without impossibility; Absurdity: a false general assertion composed of meaningless words (nonsense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat failed particular conjectures as errors; treat general false assertions that are meaningless as absurdities. Avoid forming universal claims that are inconceivable or composed of senseless words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Absurdity — 1: want of Method (no definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurd conclusions often arise from lack of method — beginning ratiocination without first settling definitions (settled significations of words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always begin reasoning from clear definitions; otherwise calculations are like casting up numbers without knowing the value of 'one, two, three'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Absurdity — 2: giving names of Bodies to Accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling accidents or properties by the names of bodies (or vice versa) produces absurdities (e.g., saying 'Faith is infused' treats a non-bodily accident as if it were bodily).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the ontological category of what you name clear—do not treat accidents as bodies or as if they could be acted upon like bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Absurdity — 3: attributing outer-accidents to our own bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascribing the accidents of bodies outside us to accidents of our own bodies (e.g., 'the colour is in the body' vs. 'the colour in the perceiver') leads to confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between the properties of external objects and the sensations/conceptions inside the perceiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Absurdity — 4: giving names of Bodies to Names (reifying universals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating names or universals as if they were bodies or real generical things (e.g., 'There be things universal' as if universals were things) creates category error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hypostatizing names into substances; keep speech's referents and the status of universals clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Absurdity — 5: giving names of Accidents to Names and Speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascribing accidents to names/speeches (e.g., 'The nature of a thing is in its definition') confuses sign and signified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that definitions and names are tools for signifying, not the ontological seat of a thing's nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Absurdity — 6: misuse of Metaphors and Tropes in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Using metaphors and rhetorical figures in place of proper words causes error in truth-seeking, even though such figures may be acceptable in common speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In serious reckoning and seeking of truth, avoid metaphors and tropes; use literal, properly defined terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Absurdity — 7: use of meaningless scholastic terms (names that signify nothing)
rubrics_metrics.description: School-cant and learned coinages without clear meaning (e.g., 'Hypostatical', 'Transubstantiate') are causes of absurd assertions because they often signify nothing intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject unexamined technical jargon; require clear explication of any term before admitting it into reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science attained by industry (imposing names and method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is not innate like sense or memory but is attained by industry: apt imposing of names and getting a good and orderly method from elements (names) to assertions and syllogisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To build science, impose appropriate names, establish definitions, and develop methodical progression from elements to conclusions; science yields knowledge of consequences and how to produce effects when causes are in our power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of Science (certainty vs uncertainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of science include some that are certain and infallible and some that are uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between infallible and merely probable signs when assessing whether a body of knowledge qualifies as science; favor methods that lead to certain, demonstrable consequences (as in geometry).
